alternate_names: family fork (when it hits king, queen and rook)
knowledge_type_note: A named variant of the fork, kept separate because the knight's geometry makes it behave differently from every other forking piece.

history.notes: A descriptive name of long, anonymous usage.

engine_era_note: Wholly mechanical and unaffected by engine-era revision. findMotifs() in this repository detects it as part of its general fork test.

preconditions: A knight attacks two or more enemy units after the move
indicators_for: One target is the king, making the fork absolute
A target is undefended or outranks the knight
The landing square cannot be attacked by an enemy pawn
The classic c7/f7 geometry against a king and a corner rook
indicators_against: The landing square is defended and the knight is simply lost
Both targets are defended and cheaper than the knight
The defender has a check or stronger counter-threat first
false_positive_traps: The landing square must be safe. This base's fork controlled pair shows the same knight move at +7.39 and at +0.57 depending only on whether one bishop guards the square.
A knight attacking two defended pawns is not a fork worth reporting.

typical_plans: Manoeuvre the knight towards a square from which it forks
Force the enemy pieces onto squares of one colour, which is the geometry a knight fork needs
Decoy a piece onto a forking square with a sacrifice
typical_moves: Nc7+ and Nf7 forking king and rook
typical_pawn_structures: Structures where the knight has an outpost within forking range
typical_piece_arrangements: King and rook on squares of the same colour, a knight's move apart
strategic_consequences: An outpost within forking distance of the king is worth more than one that is not

exceptions: A knight fork on a guarded square wins nothing.
Only another knight can attack a knight back without moving, which is why knight-versus-knight forks behave differently.
limitations: Detecting the geometry is mechanical; deciding it wins material requires resolving the exchange.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET, and the search that failed is worth recording. Five famous games were replayed through this base's own move generator and scanned position by position with the API - the Opera Game, the Evergreen, the Immortal, the Game of the Century and Legall's Mate, 225 plies between them - and this concept was not reported in any of them. That is not evidence the motif is rare; it is evidence that the five games this base can currently verify do not contain a clean instance of it, and that adding one means adding a game rather than looking harder at these. tools/replay_game.js is the instrument: a move list that is wrong is refused rather than guessed at. RESOLVED: Ed. Lasker-Alekhine, Scheveningen 1913, 30...Nxf2+, above.
misconceptions: That a knight fork always wins material. The landing square's safety decides it.
That the family and royal fork are distinct motifs. They are the same motif with more expensive targets.

examples.note:
THE MASTER-GAME RUNG. 30...Nxf2+ checks the king on h1 and attacks the rook on d1 in the same move, which is the geometry this record is named for: a knight that hits two things cannot be answered by defending either, and cannot be blocked or attacked back except by another knight.

Stockfish 18 at depth 30 with three lines: MATE IN 10, and the continuation is a second knight move rather than the capture - 31.Kg1 Nfd1, the other knight arriving. That is worth showing beside the fork, because the reason the fork wins here is not the rook. Both black knights end up in White's position and the king cannot answer both.

WHAT THE CARD MUST NOT SAY. The second-best move is +29.61 - also completely winning. Black was already winning before the fork and the fork is the fastest finish rather than the difference between winning and not. A record whose only example is a move that wins a won game teaches that forks decide games; this note says what the engine says.

counterexamples.note: The same knight arriving on the same square with b7 empty: Nd6+ is a check and nothing more. Two squares attacked, one of them a king, is not a fork - a fork needs two things worth taking, and this base does not call a check a fork merely because the knight also eyes an empty square. The page's own findMotifs tags the paired position and not this one.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Nxa7. The negative half of the pair: with b7 empty, Nd6+ attacks a king and an empty square, and this base does not call that a fork. The result is the same as in the positive half, which is the point - the pair isolates whether the FORK is present, not whether anyone is winning, and a pair whose halves differed in result would be testing the wrong thing.

ambiguous_examples.note: Shipped puzzle en-d6905ae15c. Nc4+ forks the king on b6 and the queen on a5, it is the best move on the board, it wins a queen - and the position is a PROVEN DRAW. White is two knights and a pawn against a queen and a rook, and the fork is what holds the balance rather than what wins it. Filed as ambiguous because everything the concept promises is delivered - the geometry, the double attack, the material - and the outcome is nothing. This record's other constructed example makes the same point with five men and no advantage at all; this one makes it in a real position where the fork is essential.

by_level.beginner: The knight attacks two pieces at once. They cannot both move, and nothing can block a knight.
by_level.intermediate: A knight fork. Check the square the knight lands on is safe first — that is what decides whether it wins anything.
by_level.advanced: The knight attacks the opposite colour to the square it stands on, so a forked piece can never defend itself by attacking back. Nothing interposes either.
by_level.master: Geometry first: get the enemy pieces onto one colour and the knight within range. The forking square's safety is the whole condition.

by_depth.short: The knight hits two things at once.
by_depth.normal: A knight fork: one knight attacks two or more pieces, and neither interposition nor counter-attack defends, because a knight cannot be blocked and attacks the opposite colour to the one it occupies.
by_depth.deep: The most dangerous form of fork, for three reasons rooted in the knight's move. It attacks squares of the opposite colour to the one it stands on, so a forked piece cannot defend itself by attacking back — only another knight can. Its move is the hardest to visualise, so these are the tactics most often missed. And it cannot be blocked, so interposition is never a defence. The classic squares are c7 and f7 against a king and a corner rook. The conditions for it to win material are the fork's general ones and they bite hard: in a controlled test the same Nc7+ is worth +7.39 with the landing square free and +0.57 with one bishop guarding it.

explanations.lesson: When you see a knight fork, check the square it lands on before you check anything else.

avoid: a knight fork always wins material

definition_short: A fork delivered by a knight — the most dangerous kind, because no other piece can be defended against it by standing next to it.
definition_long:
The fork's most common and most dangerous form. Three properties of the knight's move are responsible.

First, the knight attacks squares of the OPPOSITE colour to the one it stands on, so a forked piece can never simply defend itself by attacking the knight back — except another knight. Second, its move is the hardest to visualise, so knight forks are the tactics most often missed. Third, the knight cannot be blocked, so interposition is never a defence.

The archetypal squares are c7 and f7 (c2 and f2 mirrored), where a knight forks the king and a rook in the corner. When king, queen and rook are hit at once, the result is often called a FAMILY FORK; when it is king and queen, a ROYAL FORK. Both names are attested and neither is essential.

The conditions for it to WIN are the fork's general ones, and they matter as much here: the landing square must be safe, and at least one target must be undefended or worth more than the knight. A knight fork on a defended square wins nothing, and this base contains an engine-tested controlled pair demonstrating exactly that — the same Nc7+ swings 6.82 pawns depending on whether one bishop covers the landing square.
